Today’s PantryLog update focused on making the service more practical for real daily use.
PantryLog started as a simple pantry management tool for tracking bulk ingredients and refilling smaller containers. The original goal was to solve a very realistic household problem: not realizing that the main bottle or bulk product is almost empty until the moment I need to refill a smaller container.
With today’s update, PantryLog has grown beyond a basic MVP. I focused on improving five key areas: shopping list sharing, mobile usability, opened-date tracking, activity history, and data backup.
These changes make PantryLog feel much closer to a complete everyday web service.
An information indication has been added about how long the groceries have been opened
Shopping List Text Copy and Mobile Sharing
The first major improvement was making the shopping list easier to use outside the app.
PantryLog already detects items that fall below the minimum stock level and adds them to the shopping list. However, in real life, a shopping list is often shared through apps like KakaoTalk, Notes, or other messaging tools.
To support this behavior, I added a text formatting feature for low-stock items.
Now, PantryLog can automatically format the shopping list into a clean text format that is easy to copy and paste. Users can copy the list with one click and send it to another app.
I also added mobile native sharing support using the Web Share API. On supported mobile devices, users can open the native share menu and send the shopping list directly through messaging apps, notes, or other installed applications.
This small feature makes PantryLog much more useful in real shopping situations.

Mobile Responsive UI and Bottom Sheet Modals
The second major focus was mobile usability.
Since PantryLog is meant to be used in a kitchen, grocery store, or daily household environment, mobile support is especially important. A pantry management service should not only look good on a desktop screen. It should also feel natural on a smartphone.
I optimized the layout for a 375px mobile viewport and improved the dashboard design. The statistics cards now form a clean 2x2 grid on small screens, making the main information easier to read without unnecessary scrolling.
I also improved the category tabs so they work better with touch-based horizontal scrolling. This makes it easier to switch between item categories on a phone.
Another important UI improvement was converting modals into mobile-style bottom sheets. Instead of showing desktop-like popups on a small screen, PantryLog now displays certain modals from the bottom, similar to a native mobile app.
This makes the mobile experience feel more natural and polished.

Opened Date Tracker
The third feature added today was opened-date tracking.
For pantry items, simply knowing the remaining amount is not always enough. Some products may still have enough quantity left, but they may have been opened for a long time. This is especially important for ingredients such as sauces, oils, condiments, and other food items that should ideally be used within a recommended period after opening.
To handle this, I added an opened-date tracker.
When an item has an opened date, PantryLog calculates how many days have passed since it was opened and displays a badge such as:
Opened for 25 days
The system can also show warning badges when an item is close to or past its recommended usage period.
This helps users manage not only stock quantity, but also product freshness and quality.
With this feature, PantryLog becomes more than a “how much is left?” tracker. It also helps answer the question, “Is this still within a good usage period?”

Activity History Timeline
The fourth major improvement was the activity history log.
PantryLog now records important item actions, including:

• Refill deductions

• Main product restocking

• New item registration
Each action is saved with a timestamp, allowing users to review what happened to an item over time.
I also added a history button to each item card. When users click the history button, they can open a timeline popup and see the item’s recent activity.
This feature makes PantryLog more transparent and useful. Instead of only showing the current state of an item, the app now shows how that state changed.
For example, users can check when they last refilled a small bottle, when they restocked the main container, or when a product was first added.
This gives the service a stronger sense of continuity.

Data Backup and Restore
The fifth major feature was data backup and restore.
Since PantryLog currently stores data in localStorage, users need a way to protect their records. If browser data is deleted or the user changes devices, the stored pantry data could be lost.
To reduce that risk, I added an export and import feature.
Users can now download their PantryLog data as a JSON backup file named:
pantrylog_backup.json
They can also restore their data later by uploading the backup file.
This makes the service safer and more reliable, especially for users who want to keep their pantry records over time.
Even though PantryLog is still a lightweight web application, this backup feature gives users more control over their own data.

What This Update Means for PantryLog
Today’s update was not about one large feature. Instead, it was about improving the overall practicality of the service.
The shopping list can now be copied and shared more easily. The mobile UI feels more like a real app. Opened-date tracking helps users manage freshness. Activity history makes item changes easier to understand. Backup and restore support improves data safety.
Together, these features make PantryLog much more complete.
The project started as a simple MVP for tracking bulk pantry items and refill usage. Now, it is becoming a more realistic household management service that supports daily routines, mobile use, quality control, and data protection.
For me, this update was meaningful because it showed how small practical features can greatly improve the value of a service.
A useful app is not only about having a good core idea. It also needs to fit naturally into the user’s real-life workflow.
With this update, PantryLog feels much closer to that goal.
